headline: Israel weighs duties on Canadian medical cannabis in new dumping case
dek: Israel's trade levies commissioner has named four Canadian growers, led by a Cronos venture, in a dumping case; a duty decision was pending on 11 November.
key_points: Israel is weighing anti-dumping duties on Canadian medical cannabis flower for the second time in two years, MJBizDaily reported on 11 November; a decision was still pending.
On 22 October Israel's commissioner for trade levies named four exporters, led by Cronos GrowCo, which he said supplied more than 60% of Canada's exports to Israel.
The commissioner put the dumping margin at about 125%, comparing an export price of 4.43 shekels a gram with a Canadian price of about 10 shekels; Cronos says it does not dump.
Israel approved duties of up to 165% in April 2025, but the finance minister blocked them; any new duty again needs both the economy and finance ministers to agree.
body: Israel is again close to deciding whether to put punitive tariffs on medical cannabis grown in Canada. Trade officials are considering anti-dumping duties after Israeli growers complained that Canadian licensed producers sell flower into Israel below what it costs at home, MJBizDaily reported on 11 November. A decision was still pending as of that day.

The case matters well beyond Israel. Israel took about 15% of Canada's cannabis flower exports in 2025, according to MJBizDaily, and growers in Portugal and Australia have made similar complaints about cheap Canadian product, although Israel is the only country to open a formal case. A duty would raise the cost of selling into one of Canada's most important export markets at the moment the industry is leaning on exports to offset a weak domestic market.

On 22 October, Israel's commissioner for trade levies, Danny Tal, named four Canadian exporters. The largest is Cronos GrowCo, a greenhouse grower in Kingsville, Ontario, that is half owned and controlled by Cronos Group; Tal said it supplied more than 60% of Canada's cannabis exports to Israel. The others are Koots Canna in British Columbia, Cielo Verde Quebec, and 2323414 Alberta, a wholly owned subsidiary of CannaPharmaRx. Israeli officials estimate the four supply about 70% of the cannabis Israel imports from Canada.

When Tal reopened the case on 5 August, he estimated the dumping margin at about 125%, comparing an export price of 4.43 shekels a gram with a Canadian price of about 10 shekels. By MetaFlora's arithmetic, that means the flower was landing in Israel at about 44% of its home-market price. A Cronos spokesperson told MJBizDaily the company does not engage in dumping. Koots Canna declined to comment, and the other two companies did not respond.

The complainants, Evergreen Solomon Pharma and Trichome, filed on 28 May 2026, and the commissioner opened the investigation on 29 June, according to an analysis by the Israeli law firm Gornitzky. The products covered are cannabis flowers for medical use, or for use as raw material for medical purposes, containing THC, CBD or CBN. The growers say 18 Israeli producers have stopped operating, while Israeli data shows imports from Canada rose 42% in 2025.
> Canada's export model depends on selling abroad for less than it costs to sell at home; the Israel case is the first formal test of whether that is legal.
## The last attempt failed at the finance ministry

This is Israel's second try. In a case the commissioner opened on his own initiative in January 2024, Israel found dumping margins of 63% to 554%, and the economy minister signed off on duties of up to 165% in April 2025. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich blocked them later that month after the Health Ministry and the Competition Authority warned that patients would pay more. Under Israeli law, a duty needs the approval of both ministers.

Gornitzky notes that the finance minister argued at the time that Israel's market was balanced, with domestic production rising relative to imports and consumer prices falling. Israel's Competition Commissioner had also recommended against a duty, finding insufficient evidence of dumping or of a causal link to the local industry's losses. Manufacturers then asked the Jerusalem District Court to force the duty through, and the court refused to intervene. The firm also points out that the commissioner can impose a provisional measure before an investigation ends, which is the scenario exporters will be watching for now.

Cronos has more exposure than any other listed Canadian producer. Its net revenue rose 75% to US$63.5 million in the third quarter, which it attributed to flower sales in Israel and other markets, especially Germany, as we reported on 7 November. Coverage of its quarterly filing lists the Israeli anti-dumping investigation among the company's main risks.

The dumping complaint also lands in a European market where Canadian prices are already falling. Germany imported about 205 tonnes of medical cannabis in 2025, according to BfArM figures compiled by Business of Cannabis, and Canada supplied about 93 tonnes, or 46%. MJBizDaily, citing Statistics Canada trade data, reports that the declared price of Canadian flower shipped to Germany fell from C$3.95 a gram in March 2025 to C$2.93 in February 2026, a drop of about 26% by MetaFlora's calculation.

So far, German industry is not asking for trade measures. Antonia Menzel, board chair of the BPC, the German association of pharmaceutical cannabinoid companies, told MJBizDaily that import prices fell mainly because more countries are supplying Germany. An EU anti-dumping case would have to go through the European Commission and needs the backing of producers with at least 25% of EU production.

The longer-term risk for Canadian flower in Europe may be quality rules rather than tariffs. Guidance published on 8 June by the health authority in the German state of Hesse treats controlled drying as a GMP step and questions whether flower grown to GACP standards can travel long distances and be processed later without losing quality. If other regulators follow, flower grown for Canada's recreational market could lose its route into German pharmacies.

The first signal is Israel's decision on duties, including any provisional measure, and whether the finance ministry signs off this time. Global Affairs Canada told MJBizDaily it remains concerned about the dumping accusations. In Europe, watch for other German states adopting Hesse's view on drying, and for Canadian export prices in coming Statistics Canada trade releases.
